title: Soyuz (spacecraft)
description: Series of spacecraft designed for the Soviet space programme
wiki_lead:
Soyuz (Russian: Союз, IPA: [sɐˈjus], lit. 'Union') is a series of spacecraft which has been in service since the 1960s, having made more than 140 flights. It was designed for the Soviet space program by the Korolev Design Bureau (now Energia). The Soyuz succeeded the Voskhod spacecraft and was originally built as part of the Soviet crewed lunar programs. It is launched atop the similarly named Soyuz rocket from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.
Following the Soviet Union's dissolution, Roscosmos, the Russian space agency, continued to develop and use the Soyuz. Between the Space Shuttle's 2011 retirement and the SpaceX Crew Dragon's 2020 debut, Soyuz was the sole means of crewed transportation to and from the International Space Station, a role it continues to fulfill. The Soyuz design has also influenced other spacecraft, including China's Shenzhou and Russia's Progress cargo vehicle.
The Soyuz is a single-use spacecraft composed of three main sections. The descent module is where cosmonauts are seated for launch and reentry. The orbital module provides additional living space and storage during orbit but is jettisoned before reentry. The service module, responsible for propulsion and power, is also discarded prior to reentry. For added safety and aerodynamics, the spacecraft is encased within a fairing with a launch escape system during liftoff.

It was designed for the Soviet space program by the Korolev Design Bureau (now Energia). The Soyuz succeeded the Voskhod spacecraft and was originally built as part of the Soviet crewed lunar programs. It is launched atop the similarly named Soyuz rocket from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.
Following the Soviet Union's dissolution, Roscosmos, the Russian space agency, continued to develop and use the Soyuz. Between the Space Shuttle's 2011 retirement and the SpaceX Crew Dragon's 2020 debut, Soyuz was the sole means of crewed transportation to and from the International Space Station, a role it continues to fulfill. The Soyuz design has also influenced other spacecraft, including China's Shenzhou and Russia's Progress cargo vehicle.
The Soyuz is a single-use spacecraft composed of three main sections. The descent module is where cosmonauts are seated for launch and reentry. The orbital module provides additional living space and storage during orbit but is jettisoned before reentry. The service module, responsible for propulsion and power, is also discarded prior to reentry. For added safety and aerodynamics, the spacecraft is encased within a fairing with a launch escape system during liftoff.


History
The first Soyuz mission, Kosmos 133, launched unmanned on 28 November 1966. The first crewed Soyuz mission, Soyuz 1, launched on 23 April 1967 but ended tragically on 24 April 1967 when the parachute failed to deploy on reentry, killing cosmonaut Vladimir Komarov. The following flight, Soyuz 2 was uncrewed. Soyuz 3 launched on 26 October 1968 and became the program's first successful crewed mission. The program suffered another fatal setback during Soyuz 11, where cabin depressurization during reentry killed the entire crew. These are the only humans to date who are known to have died above the Kármán line, the conventional definition of the edge of space.
Despite these early tragedies, Soyuz has earned a reputation as one of the safest and most cost-effective human spaceflight vehicles, a legacy built upon its unparalleled operational history. The spacecraft has served as the primary mode of transport for cosmonauts to and from the Salyut space stations, the Mir space station, and International Space Station (ISS).


Design

Soyuz spacecraft are composed of three primary sections (from top to bottom, when standing on the launch pad):

Orbital module: A spheroid compartment providing living space for the crew.
Descent module: A small, aerodynamic capsule where the crew is seated for launch and return the crew to Earth.
Service module: A cylindrical section housing propulsion, power, and other systems.
The orbital and service modules are discarded and destroyed upon reentry. This design choice, while seemingly wasteful, reduces the spacecraft's weight by minimizing the amount of heat shielding required. As a result, Soyuz offers more habitable interior space (7.5 cubic metres, 260 cubic feet) compared to its Apollo counterpart (6.3 m3, 220 cu ft).  While the reentry module does return to Earth, it is not reusable. A new Soyuz spacecraft is made for each mission.
Soyuz can carry up to three crew members and provide life support for about 30 person-days.
A payload fairing protects Soyuz during launch and is jettisoned early in flight. Equipped with an automated docking system, the spacecraft can operate autonomously or under manual control.

grok_lead: The Soyuz (Russian: Ð¡Ð¾ÑÐ·, meaning "union") is a series of expendable crewed spacecraft originally developed by the Soviet Union in the 1960s and operated by Russia since 1991, serving as the primary vehicle for human spaceflight to low Earth orbit. It consists of three main modules: the forward orbital module, which provides additional living space and is jettisoned before reentry; the central descent module, the only part that returns to Earth and accommodates the crew during launch, orbit, and landing; and the rear service module, which supplies propulsion, power, and life support systems. Launched atop a Soyuz rocket from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan, the spacecraft is designed to carry up to three astronauts or cosmonauts for missions lasting up to several weeks, docking with space stations like the International Space Station (ISS) for crew transport and resupply. The Soyuz program originated under the leadership of Sergei Korolev, with its basic design established in 1962 as a successor to the Vostok and Voskhod spacecraft, evolving from early concepts for lunar missions to a versatile ferry for Earth orbital operations. The first uncrewed test flight occurred on November 28, 1966, followed by the inaugural crewed mission, Soyuz 1, on April 23, 1967, though it ended tragically due to technical failures. Over the decades, the design has undergone iterative improvements, including enhanced avionics, better docking mechanisms for international compatibility, and upgraded reentry systems, with variants like Soyuz-TM and the current Soyuz MS series incorporating digital controls and improved crew safety features. Soyuz has flown more than 140 missions, making it the longest-operational and most-flown human-rated spacecraft in history, with a demonstrated reliability exceeding 98% for launches and operational success rates around 95-98% for the vehicle itself. It played pivotal roles in landmark events, such as the 1975 Apollo-Soyuz Test Projectâthe first international crewed space missionâand has been essential to the ISS program since 2000, providing the sole means of crew transport after the Space Shuttle's retirement in 2011 until the introduction of commercial vehicles like Crew Dragon. Despite occasional incidents, including two fatal missions in the 1960s and 1970s, its robust design and continuous refinements have ensured its status as a cornerstone of global space exploration, with ongoing use projected into the 2020s.
